name: DevOps engineer
summary: DevOps and site reliability interviews usually cover Linux, networking, CI/CD, containers and at least one cloud platform, and lean heavily on troubleshooting: you're described a broken or slow system and asked how you'd find the problem. Candidates commonly report scripting tasks, questions on infrastructure as code and monitoring, and for SRE roles, discussion of incidents, on-call and reliability targets.
rounds: Technical screen on Linux, networking and scripting, often with a short coding or shell task
Troubleshooting round: talk through how you'd debug a failing service or server
CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes and cloud discussion, often based on setups you've built
Design round for experienced roles: a reliable deployment or infrastructure setup
Hiring manager or behavioural round on incidents and teamwork
looks_for: A methodical troubleshooting approach, from symptom to root cause
Strong Linux and networking basics: processes, files, DNS, TCP and HTTP
Automating instead of repeating manual steps: scripts, pipelines, infrastructure as code
Monitoring and alerting that catches problems before users do
Safe changes: rollbacks, gradual rollouts and least-privilege access

questions.text: Tell me about an outage you helped resolve. Walk me through the timeline.
covers: How it was detected and how badly users were affected
What you checked, in what order, and what turned out to matter
The fix, the review afterwards, and what changed as a result

questions.text: Describe a manual process you automated. What did it save?
covers: The process and why it was slow or risky
The script, pipeline or tool you built, and how you got people to use it
Time saved or errors avoided, with a number

questions.text: Tell me about a change you made that broke something. How did you handle it?
covers: What you changed and what broke
How quickly you noticed, rolled back and told people
The safeguard you added: a review step, a test, a staged rollout

questions.text: Tell me about a time developers pushed back on a process or tool you introduced.
covers: Their concern, and whether it was fair
How you adjusted the change or explained it better
Whether it was adopted, and what you learned

questions.text: A website starts returning 502 errors. Talk me through how you'd find the cause.
covers: Checking what changed recently and what the dashboards show
Following the request path: load balancer or proxy, web server, application processes, health checks
Reading logs, confirming the backend is up and reachable, then fixing or rolling back

questions.text: A Linux server is running slowly. Which commands and checks would you start with?
covers: CPU, memory, disk and network with tools such as top, free, df and iostat
Finding the process responsible and reading its logs
Checking for a full disk, heavy swapping or too many open connections

questions.text: Explain how DNS resolution works, and how you'd debug a 'site can't be reached' report.
covers: Resolver, root, top-level domain and authoritative servers, and caching with TTLs
Using dig or nslookup to see what's actually returned
Common causes: a wrong record, an expired domain, old answers cached after a change

questions.text: Walk me through a CI/CD pipeline you've built or used, from a commit to production.
covers: Build, test, security scan and packaging stages
How it deploys: environments, approvals and rollout strategy
How a bad release is caught and rolled back

questions.text: What's the difference between a container and a virtual machine, and what does Kubernetes add on top of containers?
covers: Containers share the host's kernel; virtual machines run their own operating system
What Kubernetes adds: scheduling, restarts, scaling and service discovery
When it's more than a small team needs

questions.text: A pod in Kubernetes keeps restarting. How would you find out why?
covers: kubectl describe and logs, including the previous container's logs
Common causes: failing health checks, running out of memory, bad configuration or missing secrets
Fixing the cause rather than only raising limits

questions.text: Why use infrastructure as code, and how do you make changes to it safely?
covers: Repeatable, reviewable infrastructure with a tool such as Terraform
Reviewing the plan before applying, and handling state carefully
Separate environments, and avoiding manual changes that drift from the code

questions.text: Compare blue-green, canary and rolling deployments. When would you use each?
covers: How each moves traffic to the new version
How fast you can roll back, and the extra cost of each
The metrics that decide whether a canary carries on

questions.text: What would you monitor for a web service, and how do you avoid alerts that nobody acts on?
covers: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation, plus a business signal such as orders
Alerting on what users feel, with a clear runbook for each alert
Reviewing noisy alerts regularly and tuning or removing them

questions.text: Explain SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, and how they change what a team works on.
covers: A measured indicator, a target for it, and the shortfall the target allows
Using the budget to balance new features against reliability work
An example target for a service you know

questions.text: How would you set up a web app's infrastructure so it survives a server, or a whole zone, going down?
covers: Several instances behind a load balancer, spread across zones
A database with replicas, backups and restores you've actually tested
Health checks, auto-scaling, and what would still fail if a whole region went down

questions.text: How do you manage secrets and access permissions in the cloud?
covers: A secrets manager or vault, never code or plain files committed to Git
Least-privilege roles for people and services, and rotating keys
Audit logs of who accessed what

questions.text: Why DevOps or SRE? What do you enjoy about this kind of work?
covers: What draws you: automation, reliability, helping developers ship faster
An example of work you enjoyed
An honest view of on-call and how you handle it

questions.text: How would you spend your first month getting to know our systems?
covers: Reading architecture notes, runbooks and recent incident reviews
Shadowing on-call and starting with small, safe changes
Spotting one repetitive task to automate and agreeing it with the team

tips: Practise troubleshooting answers in a fixed order: what changed, what the metrics show, then layer by layer.
Know the commands you'd actually type; interviewers often ask for them by name.
Build a small setup of your own: a container, a pipeline and a cloud deployment you can describe end to end.
Whenever you describe a change, mention its blast radius and how you'd roll it back.
If you hold a cloud certification, expect questions that check you've used the services, not just studied them.
Describe incidents without blaming people; focus on the system and what changed.
